newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro stocks rise slightly as Wall St steadies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro stocks rise slightly as Wall St steadies.

text.p: European stock markets recovered slightly on Wednesday after the Wall Street plunge finally halted overnight, but buying remained strictly for the brave.

Leading European bourses, which tumbled by up to almost four percent on Tuesday, all rose modestly in line with New York, where the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 27.57 points at 6,611.05 after losing almost 300 in the two previous sessions.
But markets remain far below their pre-Easter levels and analysts are trying to decide whether the great global bull run is over.

"We'll see an early mark-up because Wall Street managed to end higher but at the moment, buying is strictly for the brave," one London dealer said. "The pain may not be over for the Street and that will discourage bargain-hunters from getting too keen."
By mid morning, London's FTSE-100 index was up 0.21 percent after losing 1.51 percent on Tuesday. Continental bourses followed a similar trend.
In Paris, the CAC-40 was up 0.71 percent after shedding 2.82 percent on Tuesday while Germany's DAX, which lost 3.88 percent -- its biggest one-day fall since November -- recovered just 0.57 percent.
Wall Street painted a far from clear picture on Tuesday. While the blue-chip Dow rose, the wider market was down and the high-technology laden Nasdaq Composite closed 4.77 points easier at 1,216.93.
"The Dow is still looking vulnerable. Some people are talking about it losing four or five hundred more points," said another London dealer.
One man will play a leading role in deciding whether the recent plunge is merely a blip on an upward graph or the end to the bull run -- U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.

The U.S. central bank has already raised interest rates by 0.25 percentage points in a pre-emptive strike against inflation. The March rise was widely expected but now investors are beginning to speculate that the Fed might tighten the money supply again in May.
This could put another nail in the coffin for stocks.
The market is awaiting U.S. employment data at the end of the week for any signs of inflationary pressures which might prompt Greenspan to try to cool the economy.
"A bad payrolls number could really hurt and so everyone is wary," one dealer said.
By midmorning the FTSE-100, which lost 65 points on Tuesday, had recouped just 8.8 to 4,256.9 points.

With campaigning for the May 1 general election now in full swing, the London market is likely to react in the coming days to the likelihood that the opposition Labour party will beat the ruling Conservatives.
But dealers showed little interest in Wednesday's publication of the Conservative manifesto. "The manifesto is academic to some extent as nobody expects them to win," said one dealer.
In Germany the DAX recovered 18.95 of is 133.12 point loss on Tuesday to 3,314.88 while the CAC-40 was up 18.21 at 2,600.03. Paris lost 74.86 points on Tuesday.

The French market was also underpinned by a firmer bond market, but brokers did not exclude another downward correction in the coming weeks. Things were similar in Frankfurt, where a strong debt market helped stocks along with a stable dollar against the mark.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar was steady against the mark and shaky against the yen, although well above overnight lows at around 121.35 yen.
It fell overnight after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Japan had made progress in cutting its trade surplus, but it was important that it was not reversed.

Analysts said the Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" had also added pressure on the dollar against the yen as the key index measuring the mood of major manufacturers improved from the previous survey.
At mid morning, the dollar was at 122.40 yen, marginally lower than 122.60 at the European close on Tuesday. It firmed to 1.6718 marks from 1.6699.
Poor German data had no noticeable effect.

This showed Germany's January trade surplus was down to 5.6 billion marks compared with forecasts of 7.2 billion while the current account deficit rose to 9.3 billion marks against a forecast deficit of 3.5 billion.
"The figures were certainly disappointing, with the surplus lower and the current account higher than expected," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
CURRENCIES AT 0900 GMT
The dollar was at 1.6718 marks and 122.40 yen, compared with 1.6699 and 122.60 in late European trade on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0900 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 8.8 points, or 0.21 percent, at 4,256.9
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 18.21 points, or 0.71 percent, at 2,600.03.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 18.95 points, or 0.57 percent, at 3,314.88.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $350.70 an ounce compared with Tuesday's close of $350.45. Silver was seven cents lower at $4.97.
